Netflix shares sink on earnings after a dramatic content executive shake-up
You're currently following this author!
Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.
Netflix hired Peter Rice as its new content chief as co-CEO Ted Sarandos tries to boost growth.
Frank Micelotta/Tubi via Getty Images; Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Chris Pizzello/AP
Netflix's third-quarter earnings failed to excite investors, a week after a major content executive shuffle and its biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
The streamer turned in results above expectations for the third quarter, but provided weak guidance for the rest of the year. Netflix said its earnings beat was primarily due to the timing of expenses.
Netflix's revenue growth slowed for a third straight quarter, and the company projected it would continue to decelerate in the fourth quarter.
Shares fell up to 6% in after-hours trading on Tuesday.
"While Netflix is growing, the pace of that growth is slowing," Forrester's Mike Proulx said. "That's a wake-up call for the company that once defined the streaming market and is now in need of growth reacceleration."
Here's how the streaming giant's Q3 financial results compared to the company's forecast:
Revenue: $12.87 billion vs $12.86 billion estimated ($11.5 billion in Q3 2025)
Earnings: $0.87 per share vs $0.82 per share estimated ($0.59 per share in Q3 2025)
Netflix told investors to expect earnings of $0.67 per share in the fourth quarter, below Wall Street's $0.73 per share estimate. The company's $13.44 billion revenue projection for Q4 was also lower than analysts' estimate of $13.51 billion.
The streaming leader cut its annual advertising forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of its ad products.
Want more Business Insider in your news feed?
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it's concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business," said analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer, Business Insider's sister company.
Heading into Q3 earnings, Netflix's stock was down over 44% in the last year as investors worried about engagement growth and stiff competition from YouTube and other free streamers.
Netflix said in its third-quarter shareholder letter that it knows "there's some investor concern about our view hours growth" but added that engagement "remains healthy."
"We do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we're confident we'll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing" its strategy, the shareholder letter said.
The company has invested in video games and podcasts but didn't mention either in its letter, outside a disclosure section on "forward-looking statements."
Netflix's results came less than a week after it shook up its content leadership team and cut about 1,000 workers.
Content chief Bela Bajaria is leaving her role after more than three years, Netflix announced last week. The company said Monday that film chief Dan Lin is also out.
Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney exec who ran Disney's TV division, including ABC and FX. Netflix hasn't yet said who will replace Lin; Rice will oversee film in the meantime.
"It's our goal to go from very good to great," co-CEO Greg Peters said of Netflix's content slate on the company's earnings call.
The leadership changes come as Netflix battles slowing viewership growth. The streaming powerhouse generated 97 billion viewing hours in the first half of the year, which was up 2% year-over-year.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said at an industry event hosted by Bloomberg last month that Netflix was "not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster."
"Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge, but it is a worthwhile start," Benes said.
Netflix layoffs were across its product, tech, HR, and legal teams. Co-CEOs Sarandos and Peters said in a memo to staffers that the company was downsizing so it can be "disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources."
Other media companies have laid off employees in the last month. NBCUniversal cut a few hundred global streaming tech employees in early October, and Disney trimmed its tech and HR teams in late September.
In the second quarter, Netflix's results were roughly in line with analysts' expectations. The stock sank 8% after the report as Netflix said it would cut back on how frequently it shared viewership data.

Netflix stock falls 4% as slowing revenue growth raises investor concerns
This score is generated through AI-driven analysis of the article's content.
Ananthu C UAnanthu C.
Buy Netflix (NFLX). The quarter beat on EPS and revenue, margins jumped to 34.6%, and free cash flow rose to $2.9B—real fundamentals, not just hype. The selloff is driven by slower growth guidance and ad delays, which can be noisy and timing-related. With churn ~2% (industry-low) and retention holding, the core subscription engine is intact while management resets content leadership and pushes live sports/podcasts/games to lift viewing hours.
Key Risk: Content reset fails—viewing hours keep sliding and churn rises, forcing a sustained growth downgrade.
Sell Netflix (NFLX) and rotate into YouTube/Alphabet (GOOGL) or Disney+ (DIS). Nielsen shows Netflix’s US TV share (7.8%) far below YouTube (~14%), and viewing growth is weak (only ~2% more programming watched in H1 2026). If Netflix can’t quickly convert content changes into engagement, the market will keep paying competitors for stronger attention and ad momentum while Netflix’s ad rollout disappoints.
Key Risk: Netflix proves engagement inflects fast—viewing hours and ad revenue re-accelerate, and the relative underperformance reverses.
See more Invezz stories on GoogleAdd Invezz to your preferred sourcesAdd
Netflix fell 4% after hours as its revenue growth outlook weakened.
Netflix cut its 2026 ad revenue forecast to $2.7 billion.
1. Leadership changes and slowing viewing hours add to investor concerns.
Netflix shares NFLX fell around 4% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after the streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts’ expectations but forecast slower revenue growth for the fourth consecutive quarter.
The company reported revenue of $12.9 billion for the quarter, up 12% from a year earlier and in line with Wall Street expectations.
Earnings reached 87 cents per share, beating analysts’ estimates of 82 cents. Net income increased approximately 43.5% year over year to $3.66 billion.
However, Netflix forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, below analysts’ expectations.
The company also projected full-year 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion, representing 13% growth and slightly below the midpoint of its previous forecast range of 13% to 14%.
The outlook comes as Netflix faces questions about viewer engagement, advertising growth and the quality of its programming.
Netflix forecasts slower revenue growth as advertising disappoints
Netflix’s revenue growth has slowed from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of last year to a projected 11.5% in the final three months of 2026.
The company attributed the advertising shortfall partly to a slower-than-expected rollout of some products for advertisers.
Netflix now expects advertising revenue of $2.7 billion this year, compared with its previous projection of approximately $3 billion.
The company said subscription revenue growth had exceeded its expectations.
The company’s operating margin improved to 34.6% in the third quarter from 28.2% a year earlier.
Free cash flow also increased to $2.9 billion from $2.66 billion in the same period last year.
Despite these improvements, investors remain focused on Netflix’s ability to sustain growth.
The company said in its shareholder letter that it recognised investor concerns about viewing hours but remained confident it could accelerate growth in time spent watching its content.
Netflix is expanding into live sports, podcasts and video games while adding third-party film and television programming.
The company is also seeking to increase engagement as competition for viewers intensifies across streaming platforms and other digital entertainment services.
Leadership changes follow concerns over programming quality
Netflix has made significant changes to its workforce and leadership as it seeks to improve its content offering.
Over the past week, the company cut approximately 6% of its workforce, or around 1,000 positions, and removed Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin from their roles.
The company appointed Peter Rice, a veteran film and television executive who previously held senior positions at Walt Disney and 21st Century Fox, to replace Bajaria.
The changes follow growing concerns that Netflix has struggled to deliver major television and film hits capable of attracting widespread attention.
Its Emmy Awards haul fell to a 10-year low in 2026, while viewing activity has shown signs of slowing.
Netflix remains a leading global streaming platform, with more than 325 million subscribers.
However, ratings tracker Nielsen puts its share of US television viewing at 7.8%, compared with approximately 14% for YouTube.
According to figures cited by The Wall Street Journal, Netflix viewers watched only 2% more programming in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier.
Stock faces pressure as investors reassess growth prospects
Netflix shares have faced sustained pressure following the company’s unsuccessful bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery’s film and television studios and HBO Max.
The stock has fallen approximately 25% this year and more than 40% over the past year, according to the supplied reports.
Investor attention is increasingly centred on the company’s ability to increase viewing hours and generate growth without a major acquisition.
Netflix’s customer retention remains relatively strong. Research firm Antenna estimated that its subscription churn rate was around 2% in September, unchanged from August and the lowest in the industry.
The company also said customer responses to price increases this year were in line with expectations, indicating that engagement remained healthy.
Nevertheless, the weaker advertising outlook and slowing revenue growth have added to concerns about its near-term performance.
Netflix’s improving margins and cash flow provide some support, but investors will be watching whether its content strategy and new entertainment offerings can translate into stronger viewing activity and sustained growth.

Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement, revenue growth
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:41 PM CDT 3 min read
California-based streaming giant Netflix saw shares drop amid concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth (JUSTIN SULLIVAN)
Netflix stock dropped more than five percent Tuesday afternoon after its quarterly earnings release failed to assuage investor concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how the company measures engagement, and added that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.
The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streamers, gaming and sports.
Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months" and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes," John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.
In its third quarter ending in September, Netflix recorded $12.87 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.
It did not provide overall figures for subscriber view hours in the quarter, but noted that in India the metric increased 24 percent compared to the same period last year.
In July, Netflix said subscribers spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a 2 percent increase over the first half of 2025.
It stopped reporting subscriber numbers in the first half of 2025.
But the company touted growth outside the US while acknowledging challenges stateside.
"We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working," co-CEO Ted Sarandos told investors on an analyst call Tuesday, highlighting engagement, subscribers, revenue and profits across Latin America, Europe and Asia.
"The U.S. is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos continued.
The company will also reportedly cut around 6 percent of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, according to media reports.
Among them were seven high-level employees in charge of television deals and content, the Hollywood Reporter reported last week.
The company also recently replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who oversaw popular shows including "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton," and "Squid Game," in addition to pushing the company's live entertainment strategy, according to CNBC.
Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice to be its new content chief.
"Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work," Sarandos said on the call Tuesday.
Competition from other streamers has forced Netflix to work harder to attract and retain both paid and ad-supported members.
The company has increasingly dipped into live sports -- with agreements to stream major events like the Olympics and World Cup -- in addition to gaming and shorter-form content. The NFL and WWE are also on board to stream live events.
In the US, it reached 7.8 percent of streaming television viewers in July compared to YouTube's 14.2 percent, a record for the Google-owned site, according to media analytics firm Nielsen.
The World Cup lifted overall television viewership in July, according to Nielsen.
"It's really important to remember, roughly 95 percent of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core, where we see a long runway for future growth," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call, emphasizing its commitment to traditional television and film content.
The company also missed expectations on advertising revenue growth.
"We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing" on advertising, nonetheless, co-CEO Greg Peters said on the call.
"We see the benefits when we continue to roll out other products like new ad formats, which help with our growth," Peters added.

35 Analysts Bullish, 15 on the Fence: What Netflix Needs to Show This Quarter
Netflix reports Q3 earnings on October 20 with shares sitting near a 52-week low and analysts split between conviction and caution. Whether the quarter calms those nerves or deepens them depends on a few specific numbers management has already put…
Published October 20, 2026, 8:45am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
The Netflix corporate campus, featuring its iconic red logo, as the company faces significant job cuts and leadership changes. © JasonDoiy / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
Third-quarter results from Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) are due on October 20 after the close. Shares head in at $70.53. The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Netflix is $81.75, which means 15.91% upside. The stock earns a buy rating with high confidence from the model.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
Wall Street leans the same way. Netflix has 7 Strong Buy, 28 Buy, 15 Hold and 1 Sell ratings, and the consensus target is $91.39.
Management guided Q3 to revenue of $12.86B and EPS of $0.82. Consensus stands at $0.8229 and $12.88 billion, so Netflix needs a clean beat on both lines.
A 40% Slide Sets a Low Bar Heading Into Earnings
Over the past year the stock has lost 40.41%, including a 24.78% drop year to date and a 7.7% decline over the past month. It is up 0.33% for the week. That leaves shares much closer to the $65.08 52-week low than to the $124.86 high. On Friday the stock fell 2.86% after Netflix, a Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) rival, replaced its content chief with a former Disney executive.
In Q2, revenue grew 13.4% to $12.56B, slightly missing expectations. EPS of $0.80 came in ahead of the $0.79 consensus. Even so, shares fell 7.26% on the day. This stock has been punished hard for misses, with an average response of -9.89%.
Our one-year bull case is $119.90. Advertising is expected to roughly double to about $3B in 2026. Management says the revenue gap between the ad tier and the ad-free plan “is narrowing.”
Netflix also has $27.1B left on its buyback authorizations, and it reaches less than 45% of an estimated 800 million addressable households. Full-year guidance still calls for operating margin of 31.5%.
Our bear case is $74.80. Q2 free cash flow fell to $1.53B from $2.27B. Higher cash taxes explain part of that drop, and full-year guidance still points to about $12.5B.
View hours grew only 2% in the first half. A change in content leadership adds execution risk, and $1B of debt needs refinancing this year.
Netflix Earns a Premium Over Its Streaming Rivals
Disney is the most direct competitor in streaming, and Disney+ and Hulu SVOD operating income more than doubled to $712 million last quarter. Disney trades at a lower multiple, though its operating margin is roughly half of Netflix’s.
Spotify Technology (NYSE:SPOT) runs a similar subscription-plus-ads model and grew revenue 13.93%, about the same rate as Netflix, yet it trades at nearly twice Netflix’s multiple.
Netflix pairs the best margins in this group with a mid-range multiple, so the comparison makes the 24/7 Wall St. price target look reasonable, arguably conservative.
What Could Move Netflix After This Report
The 24/7 Wall St. price target remains $81.75, with a buy rating and 90% confidence. The bear case still stands above today’s price.
The case strengthens if Q3 meets the 33.2% margin guide and advertising stays on rate. The case weakens if Netflix cuts full-year revenue guidance. At this valuation, the model finds more upside than downside.

These projections assume Netflix keeps executing on pricing, ads and live events. If advertising scales faster than expected, the five-year bull case reaches $238.33.

pages.title: Netflix Cut Its Ad Revenue Forecast by $300 Million. Does That Matter More Than Its Earnings Beat? | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
Netflix (NFLX -1.66%) released third-quarter earnings after hours on Tuesday, and it was another disappointment for investors. The stock was trading down 6% after hours.
While its headline numbers were slightly ahead of expectations, Netflix's engagement remained weak, and its trend of slowing growth continued. In fact, the company reported its slowest top-line growth in three years, and it expects it to continue to moderate in the fourth quarter.
Overall revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, which matched expectations, while its operating margin came in at 34% due to the timing of its content spend. On the bottom line, earnings per share improved from $0.59 to $0.87, beating estimates of $0.82.
However, beyond the existing concerns about engagement and its weak original content slate, one number underscored Netflix's troubles. The company cut its ad revenue guidance for the year from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, indicating weakness in what's supposed to be a key growth market for the streamer.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Netflix was late to launch its advertising business, finally pulling the trigger in 2022 after years of resistance. The decision has turned out to be a success, giving customers a lower-priced option and allowing advertisers to meet audiences where they are, on streaming. The two-tiered advertising model has become the norm in the streaming industry, and all of Netflix's rivals offer some version of a higher-priced ad-free tier and a lower-priced tier with ads.
Advertising was also supposed to give Netflix an avenue for growth at a time when its subscription business is believed to be maturing, especially in core markets like the U.S. Netflix no longer reports quarterly subscriber numbers, so investors don't have much insight into subscriber growth anymore.
Netflix cut its ad revenue forecast due to a "slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities," which places the blame for the shortfall on a technical issue rather than a business issue like weak demand from advertisers or poor engagement. That's a good sign for investors, but still a disappointment, nonetheless.
Is it a red flag?
Advertising still makes up a small fraction of Netflix's revenue. The streamer expects to bring in $51.1 billion in revenue this year, meaning that advertising makes up less than 6% of its revenue. The subscription business still dominates.
However, advertising is a key part of the growth story, and it could face increased scrutiny from Wall Street, especially given the disappointing engagement trends.
The advertising weakness isn't a red flag, but Netflix has become a "show-me story" this year, meaning it needs to prove to investors that it can stop its growth slowdown and improve engagement, or it will continue to face skepticism, which is likely to push the stock lower. The advertising weakness, whether it's due to a one-off technical issue or something else, only adds to those concerns.
Market capMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.$290.85B
Netflix's guidance for the fourth quarter called for revenue growth of 11.5% to $13.44 billion, and earnings per share of $0.67, both of which were below the analyst consensus of $13.52 billion in revenue and $0.73 in earnings per share.
That's still decent top-line growth, but the company desperately needs to show Wall Street that something is going right for the business, or the stock slide looks likely to continue. At one point, advertising looked like that bright spot, but unless management tells us something different in the fourth-quarter report, investors may count that as another one of many disappointments from the company over the last year.

Slowing Revenue Growth Puts Pressure On Netflix
Netflix reported Q3 earnings of $0.87 per share, beating Wall Street’s estimate of $0.82, according to Fiscal.ai. Revenue reached $12.9 billion, in line with expectations, but the company gave a weaker Q4 sales outlook. Netflix is battling slowing revenue growth for the fourth straight quarter as it faces rising competition and works to attract more viewers and grow its advertising business.

Netflix (NFLX) Stock Nears Earnings With $64–$77 Range in Focus
Netflix stock faces a key earnings test Tuesday as options signal wide price swings and analysts track revenue growth ahead of Q3.
By Maxwell MutumaOctober 19, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Netflix shares have fallen nearly 47% from their June 2025 peak, ahead of Tuesday’s earnings.
Options markets suggest Netflix stock could move approximately 9% following the third-quarter results.
BMO Capital Markets and Wedbush lowered their Netflix stock price targets before the earnings release.
Analysts expect Netflix revenue to reach $12.87 billion, with earnings of approximately $0.82 per share.
Netflix faces slower revenue growth as advertising, subscription pricing and streaming competition remain in focus.
Netflix (NFLX) shares face a test on Tuesday, October 20, when the streaming company reports third-quarter earnings. The stock closed Friday at $70.53, almost 47% below its June 2025 peak, as investors weighed slower growth and stronger competition.
Netflix Options Point to Another Price Swing
Traders expect a sharp move after the results. Short-dated options have shown implied volatility near 92.3%, compared with historical volatility of about 34%, reflecting higher prices for protection against sudden share movements.
Market estimates indicate that Netflix shares could move roughly 9% in either direction after earnings. That would place the stock near $64 or $77.
Options data also showed more calls than puts, with a reported put-to-call ratio below 0.40. Such positioning indicates demand for upside exposure, although it cannot establish which direction the stock will move.
Analysts Lower Netflix Stock Price Targets
Several analysts adjusted forecasts before the report. BMO Capital Markets reduced its price target to $125 from $135 while keeping an outperform rating. Wedbush lowered its target from $105 to $90.
Jefferies set an $85 target with a buy rating, while Huber Research downgraded the shares to sell and set a $70 target. Analysts remain divided over how quickly Netflix can increase viewing and advertising revenue.
Audience trends across digital media have also faced scrutiny. Recent Truth Social traffic estimates pointed to fewer daily users, although the figures concern a separate platform and do not measure Netflix viewing.
Analysts expect third-quarter revenue of approximately $12.87 billion, up nearly 12% from a year earlier. They forecast earnings of 82 cents per share, compared with 59 cents in the previous year.
Netflix generated $12.56 billion in second-quarter revenue, representing 13% annual growth. It now expects full-year sales between $51 billion and $51.4 billion and has projected advertising revenue near $3 billion in 2026.
Competition extends beyond subscription services. A recent streaming distribution agreement involving FreeCast shows how other providers are seeking viewers through bundled entertainment and advertising-supported programming.
Technology spending remains another industry focus. Meta’s recent AI model release came as Netflix continued using technology in content production and advertising, although their initiatives serve different purposes.

pages.title: Netflix needs blockbusters to reverse its $135 billion wipeout | The Seattle Times
pages.text:
Netflix Inc. needs to prove that it can produce hit movies and TV series again to stop a slide that has erased more than $135 billion in market value this year.
The streaming giant reports earnings after the close Tuesday, and investors will likely be more more attuned to what content executives say is coming over the next six months than the company’s third-quarter numbers.
The stock is down more than 25% in 2026, putting Netflix among the 10 worst performers in the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index and on track for its worst year since 2022, and it’s coming off a 14% decline in September. The reason is no secret to anyone following the company — user engagement has stalled due to a lack of popular content despite heavy spending driven by a crowded, competitive entertainment landscape.
The shares fell as much as 1.1% on Tuesday.
Netflix won the fewest Emmy Awards in a decade this year, and the company isn’t growing fast enough, according to Co-Chief Executive Officer Ted Sarandos.
“The content’s getting very expensive, and there’s just still too many players,” said Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management. “I think there’s so many better tech stories out there than Netflix that have sticky customers.”
Netflix is taking steps to improve its content and raise its audience numbers. On Monday, it announced that the head of its film division, Dan Lin, was leaving, and last week replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with Peter Rice, the former chairman of Walt Disney Television. The company also plans to cut about 1,000 positions in various departments globally in a bid to reduce costs.
For investors, however, the issue is this earnings report won’t reflect those moves. And even if executives give a solid revenue outlook, it’s unlikely to quell the debate around engagement, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Raganathan.
“A stronger 4Q slate could revive viewing and ads, but investors will want proof that engagement can improve without derailing margin expansion,” she wrote in an Oct. 19 note. The addition of Rice signals a potential pivot toward “more premium, conversation-driving originals and higher 2027 content spending,” she added.
Analysts following the company expect it to report a 12% rise in revenue in the third quarter to $12.9 billion, and a 39% jump in earnings to 82 cents a share, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Its gross margin is expected to be 51%, down slightly from the second quarter.
Wall Street remains generally bullish on the stock, with an average price target of about $92 suggesting a more than 30% rise over the next 12 months. And while sentiment has weakened, with two analysts putting sell-equivalent ratings on the shares in the last month, bulls see a vibe shift coming.
“While total viewing is still weak, quality has improved as reflected in hour/top-10 title and the number of sequels is increasing” through the end of the year, Oppenheimer analysts led by Jason Helfstein wrote in an Oct. 14 note. Three months of US price increases and one month of higher ad rates should give revenue a boost, and the recent headcount reductions will allow for more spending on marketing or content or provide upside to margins, they added.
Management may offer some indications for what it expects in 2027, but the company is unlikely to offer thorough guidance, according to Mark Mahaney of Evercore ISI. He was particularly enthusiastic about Netflix’s recent release of East of Eden.
“East of Eden looks very promising to us,” Mahaney wrote in a note to clients on Oct. 16. “Steinbeck is BACK!”
Ad revenue may be more important to investors than audience engagement, according to Wedbush’s Alicia Reese, who says the segment is on track to double to roughly $3 billion in 2026.
“Netflix is actively making changes that should address both its engagement issues and shift dollars from heavy infrastructure to more focused content spend,” Reese wrote in an Oct. 16 note.
One argument for buying the stock would be valuation, considering it’s priced at less than 19 times earnings projected over the next 12 months, the lowest valuation since 2022 and a steep discount to its 10-year average of 49.
That helps explain why KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Justin Patterson believes the Netflix bear case is already priced into the share price.
“The bear case on slowing engagement and more modest margin expansion is arguably priced in,” he wrote in an Oct. 12 note. “We believe management is aware of these issues, and expect to see corrective action taken across content investment and expense realignment to bolster growth and earnings, and deliver value.”

pages.title: Dan Lin Out as Netflix Film Head
pages.text:
Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images for American Cinematheque
Dan Lin is out as Netflix‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter.
The news comes as the streamer cuts from its uppermost ranks and implements layoffs that will affect roughly 1,000 people, the company’s biggest cut since 2022. Prior to Lin, chief content officer Bela Bajaria was exited, along with VP of film Doug Belgrad and a series of high-ranking television executives.
It is unclear who will assume Lin’s role, but the understanding is that Peter Rice, who took over the chief content officer post, will be in charge of finding new leadership. Netflix did not immediately reply for comment.
Lin joined Netflix in 2024, taking over from then film chief Scott Stuber. Under Stuber, Netflix became known as the place where name filmmakers could land big budgets and paydays as the traditional studios implemented more cost-conscious spending practices. During this time, the streamer consistently ended up with best picture nominations, but top awards have notoriously evaded Netflix films.
Lin, who was hired by Bajaria, was brought in to curb spending while (ideally) increasing the quality of the entire film slate, not just the titles from big-name directors.
Under Lin, the streamer‘s movies division was reorganized by genre, with deputies like Kira Goldberg, Ori Marmur and Jason Young handling films that fell under categories like sci-fi, rom-com and family film. Netflix began offering more mid-size films that have been ignored by theatrical players, including big book adaptations like Remarkably Bright Creatures and People We Meet on Vacation, as well as mid-budget action films like Apex and The RIP.
(This is not to say that Netflix’s Lin tenure was without big swings — see: Greta Gerwig‘s Narnia movie due out next year or David Fincher’s The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth— but the offerings no doubt slowed.)
Lin came from his production company Rideback, which minted the $1 billion grossing Aladdin and was involved in the hit It movies as well as The Lego Movies. He departed the company when he joined Netflix, leaving partners at the helm who found another $1 billion hit with last summer’s live-action Lilo & Stitch. Presumably, he could return to Rideback now that his Netflix tenure is up.
As of late, the streamer hasn’t been able to capture audience interest, at least at the rate co-CEO Ted Sarandos would like, with viewership and subscriber growth stagnant. Under Rice‘s leadership, Netflix will focus on “creating big, buzzy hits,“ as Sarandos wrote in his memo to staff.
After the initial news broke, Netflix confirmed the news and shared statements from Lin and Sarandos. Lin said, “It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg [Peters] and Bela for the opportunity.”
Sarandos added: “I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear. Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigor around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.”
Oct. 19, 10:16 a.m. Updated with statements from Lin and Sarandos.

pages.title: Netflix to Run Consumer Products Licensing Directly in Brazil
pages.text:
Netflix Launches Licensing Operations in Brazil
Starting in 2027, Netflix will directly manage commercial relationships with licensees in the country to develop regional consumer products.
"KPop Demon Hunters" display in Brazil. Netflix
In 2027, Netflix will start manage its consumer products licensing business in Brazil directly, working side by side with partner brands. To support this new chapter, the local team will include specialists in creative development and integrated projects to support Netflix’s stories and fandoms with brands’ expertise in products, categories and retail to deliver products and experiences.
After establishing the business through a commercial representation model, which was instrumental in building its presence in Brazil, Netflix will work more closely with licensees through a larger local team dedicated to faster decision-making, with a focus on relevance, engagement and innovation.
In practice, direct relationships will evolve the way products are developed. Partners will be able to tell Netflix directly which audiences, categories or cultural conversations they want to explore. Netflix, in turn, will identify opportunities through its knowledge of fandoms: the most talked-about characters, what went viral in the previous season and what fans want more of.
Related:'Miraculous: Ladybug & Cat Noir' Live Stage Show to Tour 15 North American Cities in 2027
“Brazil is a strategic market for our business, with passionate fans and creative partners who deeply understand their categories and local consumers,” says Paola Ogaz, director, consumer products, Latin America, Netflix. “Direct consumer products licensing operations allow us to work even more closely with partners to develop products that put fans first, are unmistakably Netflix and effectively meet brands’ business objectives
Netflix adopted this model in Mexico about a year and a half ago, and those learnings are helping inform the next chapter in Brazil. To support this new phase, the local team is expanding with specialists in creative development and projects integrated with the advertising business, which works directly with Netflix’s ad-supported plan, and brand partnerships, which develops brand campaigns on and off the screen. Both are part of the company’s commercial ecosystem, alongside consumer products.
For brands, this connection offers a way to participate in cultural universes where passion and demand already exist, driving sales and brand recall. That potential is an expression of the Netflix Effect: the ability of stories to shape culture, influence behavior and generate demand beyond the screen. With “KPop Demon Hunters,” that interest translated into products ranging from toys to food, with partners such as Candide, Grow, C&A, Renner, Riachuelo, Ediouro, Grendene, Tilibra and Knorr, alongside global brands available in the country. The results are also reflected in sales. “Stranger Things” Pringles sold three times the volume of the brand’s previous flavor innovation, across more than 17,000 points of sales, per Netflix. Comfort Segredos “Bridgerton” fabric softener exceeded initial expectations by 4.5 times, according to the company. Seara’s “Stranger Things” Upside Down pizza and the Bauducco line inspired by the Netflix brand itself are branded products that remain on shelves in Brazilian stores and supermarkets.

pages.title: Netflix Q3 profit jumps 44%, but weak advertising outlook sends shares lower
pages.text:
Netflix Q3 profit jumps 44%, but weak advertising outlook sends shares lower
Streaming major trims 2026 ad revenue forecast to $2.7 billion as slower growth and US content execution weigh on investor sentiment, viewing hours rise 24% in India
Published:
Netflix reported a 44% year-on-year increase in third-quarter profit and an 11.8% rise in revenue, marking the lowest growth rate in three years, but issued a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook, leading to a nearly 6% drop in shares.
The company lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to approximately $2.7 billion, citing delays in product rollouts and partner integrations, despite expecting over 80% growth in its advertising business this year.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos emphasized the need for better execution in the U.S. market and highlighted the importance of producing quality content to enhance subscriber engagement amid increasing competition from platforms like YouTube and TikTok.
Netflix experienced a 24% increase in viewing hours in India during the third quarter, driven by successful local content, and reported its largest quarter of paid net additions in the region.
Netflix’s third-quarter profit rose 44% year-on-year and revenue jumped 11.8% (lowest rate of increase in 3 years), but its weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook and a reduction in its full-year advertising revenue forecast triggered a fresh sell-off in its shares on Tuesday, highlighting the pressure to sustain growth as it scales up its advertising business.
Netflix reduced its advertising forecast for 2026 to roughly $2.7 billion, down from about $3 billion. Some ad product capabilities rolled out slightly slower than expected, executives said in their quarterly letter to shareholders.
Shares fell nearly 6% to $64.66 in after-hours trading on October 20. The stock had already lost more than 25% of its value over the preceding year, reflecting concerns about engagement growth, competition and the sustainability of its premium valuation.
"I know that we could do better," Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a post-earnings video call. "Now we've seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level."
Third-quarter revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, in line with Wall Street forecasts, but the lowest rate of increase in nearly ⁠three years. The company forecast fourth-quarter net income of $2.79 billion and EPS of 67 cents, below the average analyst forecast of $3.07 billion and 73 cents.
Sarandos said the company plans to focus on its core business of producing quality TV shows and movies to make Netflix a must-have service, and the recent executive shakeup was a step toward that goal. In its earnings report, Netflix said it would continue to expand its offerings through licensing more third-party ‌content.
Netflix expects fourth-quarter revenue of $13.44 billion, up 11.5% year-on-year, but forecasts net income of $2.79 billion and earnings per share of 67 cents. Both figures fall short of analysts’ expectations of $3.07 billion and 73 cents, respectively. The company also projects an operating margin of 26%, down from 34.6% in Q3.
For the full year, Netflix maintained its revenue guidance of $51.1 billion, representing approximately 13% growth, and an operating margin target of 31.5%. However, it lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast to approximately $2.7 billion from $3 billion, citing delays in rolling out advertising products and partner integrations. Despite the revision, the advertising business is expected to grow more than 80% this year, according to co-CEO Greg Peters.
For advertisers and media buyers, the revision highlights the difference between growing demand for streaming inventory and building the technology, partnerships and formats needed to monetise it at scale.
Sarandos calls for stronger US content execution
Sarandos said Netflix’s underlying strategy remained unchanged, centred on exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events, supported by licensing and global distribution.
“Our business and our business flywheel are working. There’s no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S.,” Sarandos said.
Notably, Netflix has posted monthly subscriber losses in the US throughout 2026, with no net additions reported ⁠for any month up to September, data from analytics firm Antenna showed, as reported by Reuters. Antenna tracks US subscription purchases via sources like credit card transactions, but excludes subscriptions acquired through wholesale bundles.
Sarandos acknowledged that the company had delivered “some really solid doubles and triples this year”, but said it needed more breakout hits that could travel internationally. “I know that we could do better,” he added, pointing to an opportunity to take the content slate to the next level.
Sarandos also highlighted the importance of creative talent, saying incoming chief content officer Peter Rice understood talent relations in a competitive market. Netflix recently laid off around 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and announced leadership changes involving content chief Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin.
Live sports and events remain central to the growth strategy. Sarandos said such programming can attract new members, support advertising revenue and increase value for existing subscribers. Yet competition from YouTube and TikTok, alongside questions over viewing-hour growth, puts greater pressure on Netflix to deliver stronger engagement.
The challenge now is to convert its global reach and content investments into faster growth, while improving advertising monetisation and maintaining profitability.
India is the example Netflix chose. View hours there grew 24% year over year in the third quarter, led by Lock Upp, its first daily reality series, according to the letter. Netflix recorded its largest quarter of paid net additions in India, and revenue there grew about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

Wall Street analysts are broadly bullish, with a mean price target above $90; the shares closed Monday near $70. A rise to that target would still leave the shares shy of record highs above $130, though.
But Gabelli Funds Portfolio Manager John Belton in emailed comments Tuesday called Netflix an “unloved stock.”
“Investors are concerned about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes,” he wrote.

pages.title: Netflix earnings preview: Q4 outlook, ad growth, margins in focus as stock falls 23%
pages.text:
Netflix earnings preview: Q4 outlook, ad growth, margins in focus as stock falls 23%
This score is generated through AI-driven analysis of the article's content.
Vatsala GaurVatsala G.
Buy Netflix (NFLX) ahead of earnings. The stock is down ~23% YTD, but the core investment case is intact: operating margin already ~33% and guided ~33% again, while ad revenue is expected to roughly double to ~$3B in 2026. If management confirms Q4 margin stability and shows ad monetization is accelerating (not just “starting”), the market will re-rate the earnings power and cash flow story (supporting buybacks).
Key Risk: Guidance shows margins roll over because content costs rise faster than ad growth, proving profitability can’t offset slowing revenue.
NFLX sell if growth decelerates faster than ads can replace
Sell Netflix (NFLX) if the Q4 outlook implies further deceleration (~11.7% revenue growth) without a clear step-up in ad contribution. The thesis breaks if advertising stays small relative to total sales (still ~6%) and subscription growth keeps slowing, meaning the company can’t “buy back” growth with monetization. In that scenario, valuation support from margin expansion and cash generation disappears.
Key Risk: Ad growth fails to translate into meaningful revenue acceleration, so overall growth keeps slowing and the stock de-rates.
See more Invezz stories on GoogleAdd Invezz to your preferred sourcesAdd
Netflix shares are down about 25% in 2026 as investors await Q3 results.
Q3 revenue guidance implies a deceleration to about 11.7%.
Investors will watch Q4 guidance and operating margins.
Netflix is set to report its third-quarter 2026 results after Tuesday's market close, with investors looking for signs that advertising growth and improving profitability can offset slowing revenue growth and intensifying competition from YouTube.
The streaming giant's shares have fallen approximately 23% year to date, raising the stakes for its latest earnings report as analysts reassess its growth prospects and valuation.
Attention will centre on quarterly revenue, operating margins, advertising monetisation and management's outlook for the final three months of the year.
Analysts expect Netflix to report revenue of $12.87 billion, an increase of 11.8% from a year earlier.
Revenue growth slowdown puts Q4 outlook in focus
Netflix reported revenue of $12.56 billion in the second quarter, up 13.4% year over year, while diluted earnings per share of $0.80 edged past the consensus estimate of $0.79.
For the third quarter, management guided for revenue of approximately $12.86 billion and earnings per share of $0.82, below previous Wall Street expectations.
The outlook triggered a sell-off after the company's previous results.
Revenue growth has slowed over recent quarters, falling from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 16.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and 13.4% in the second quarter.
The third-quarter revenue guidance implies further deceleration to about 11.7%.
"Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said recently at Bloomberg's 2026 Screentime event in Los Angeles.
"We are, though, also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number," he added.
Investors will thus assess whether the company can stabilise growth or whether its expansion is slowing faster than anticipated.
The fourth-quarter outlook could prove particularly important.
Netflix's full-year 2026 revenue guidance stands at $51 billion to $51.4 billion.
Advertising growth offers a potential boost
Advertising remains a key part of Netflix's strategy to diversify revenue beyond subscriptions.
The company expects its advertising business to generate approximately $3 billion in 2026, roughly double the previous year's figure.
Even so, advertising would account for only about 6% of annual sales.
Netflix has taken several steps to expand its advertising platform.
It concluded its 2026 US upfront advertising negotiations in August with commitments nearly doubling, secured its first Media Rating Council accreditation for Netflix Ads Suite and made Pause Ads available programmatically across major demand-side platforms, according to Zacks.
Investors will look for evidence that these initiatives are translating into sustained revenue growth and improving monetisation.
Jefferies maintained its Buy rating on Netflix last week, with an $85 price target, arguing that the company has significant room to expand monetisation, margins and share repurchases.
Analyst Brent Thill expects annual revenue growth of 11% between 2026 and 2029, driven by subscriber additions, price increases and advertising.
Jefferies forecasts advertising revenue rising to $7.5 billion by 2029 from $3 billion in 2026.
Thill also sees scope for further subscription price increases.
Netflix's standard plan costs about 60% less than competing services on a price-per-viewing-hour basis in the US, he noted, potentially giving the company room to raise prices.
Margin expansion remains central to the investment case
While revenue growth has slowed, Netflix's operating margins have continued to improve.
The company reported a 33.4% operating margin in the second quarter and guided for 33.2% in the third quarter.
Its full-year operating margin target stands at 31.5%, and investors will watch for any changes to that forecast.
Morningstar senior equity analyst Matthew Dolgin has identified margin expansion as a key component of the investment case.
"Ongoing margin expansion is a key component of the thesis behind investing in Netflix," Dolgin said.
The company's ability to control content costs while growing advertising revenue could help sustain profitability even as sales growth moderates.
Jefferies forecasts approximately 190 basis points of annual operating margin expansion through 2029.
Thill also expects more than $50 billion in cumulative free cash flow over three years, potentially providing substantial capacity for share repurchases.
Some analysts have sought to highlight Netflix's international opportunity amid slowing growth.
Morningstar expects Netflix to deliver a compound annual revenue growth rate of about 10% through 2030, followed by mid-single-digit growth in the latter five years of its 10-year forecast.
"We expect international markets to lead this growth, given the opportunities they still have to add new members," Dolgin wrote.
Deutsche Bank recently upgraded the stock to Buy from Hold, even though it lowered its PT to $95 from $100, with analyst Bryan Kraft noting that international engagement has increased year over year in each of the past four six-month periods.
Kraft believes Netflix's global scale, brand and production capabilities could support a broader "Netflix As A Platform" opportunity over time.
Growth across Netflix's four reported geographic regions will therefore be another important metric, particularly as international markets account for much of the remaining subscriber expansion opportunity.
Management changes and analyst downgrades add pressure
Netflix is also undergoing organisational changes.
Last week, the company announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice would become chief content officer, overseeing its global content organisation, including scripted and unscripted series, films and live events.
He will replace 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team, including its live sports strategy.
The company also announced plans on October 14 to cut approximately 1,000 jobs, or about 6% of its workforce, increasing scrutiny of cost discipline as content spending remains significant.
Recent analyst actions have reflected divided views on the stock.
Wells Fargo downgraded Netflix to Underweight in September, citing the possibility of declining viewing hours for its leading original programmes.
HSBC lowered its rating to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $76.
Deutsche Bank subsequently upgraded the stock to Buy with a $95 target, while Goldman Sachs maintained its Buy rating with a $90 target.
KeyBanc, Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Huber Research have also lowered their price targets this month.
For Netflix, Tuesday's results will test whether advertising growth and margin expansion can offset slowing sales and heightened competition.
Investors will also look for signs that the company's international growth, pricing power and cash generation can sustain earnings expansion over the coming years.

Netflix Sales Growth to Decline for Fourth Quarter in a Row
Netflix reported earnings for the third quarter that exceeded Wall Street expectations, but forecast a fourth consecutive quarter of slowing sales growth, a projection that may amplify concerns about the performance of the world's leading online TV network. Netflix delivered sales of $12.9 billion in the third quarter, in line with Wall Street's expectations, and forecast sales of $13.4 billion in the year's final three months, falling short of what analysts have predicted. The pace of growth has fallen from 17.6% in the final quarter of last year to a projection of 11.5% for this year's fourth quarter. The company blamed its sales shortfall on the advertising business, which is on pace to deliver $300 million less than the company expected. Bloomberg Tech Host Ed Ludlow joins Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss. He speaks with Alexis Christoforous and Norah Mulinda.
First blush doesn't look too good, Ed. What is catching your eye?

It doesn't really tell the story, right? They're just numbers on the Netflix side. So, uh, you know, it's not a company that gives subscribers anymore. The growth is measured against revenues and then by extrapolation, how much revenue they might book for one particular viewer of their audience. But if you don't have the latter part, it's hard.
Um, but you know, basically, it's a very simple story where numbers are bang in line or slightly below expectations. And when you're closing out a year, uh, and you're telling investors, this is the balance of the year, there's no upside, hence the the stock down 6%.

there was an admission very recently, you guys will remember at Bloomberg Screen Time from co-CEO Ted Sarandos that growth is not where Netflix wants it to be. But based on the numbers that they just printed for the quarter gone, and looking for the balance of 26, the guide that they're giving us, sales growth is going to decline for a fourth straight quarter. So whatever they're doing to change things, it's not happening yet, right? It's not um resulted in in something yet.
Is that really what we're going to hear from the uh, from the conference call? Uh the fact that, hey, listen, we just implemented these changes. We just laid, we had the most layoffs in our company's history. We're changing people in the big decision-making offices. I mean, like, give it time. Are they going to ask for Wall Street to be patient?
I think they kind of go back to what Netflix always says, which is um, the content slate and uh, content slate on a quality basis and content slate on a on a volume basis. Um, one of the things that they've struggled with, I heard that you uh

I just finished The Gentleman season 2.
Oh, I'm so far behind on that.
So, so the Gentleman season 3 is shooting right now, right now. Other than the three of us just chatting about what we like to watch, what's the story for Netflix? Actually, they've struggled to keep the audience across seasons. So you might have a big hit. Season one, great success, right, by their own measurements that they disclose. But then the audience doesn't stick with those season two and season three for whatever reason. And and some remedy to that's kind of important. So maybe that that's kind of a line of questioning on the content side.
And I guess, you know, they'll they'll be asked maybe directly what the those changes in key leadership personnel will mean for for for that that content slate.
I mean, I'm looking through some of the numbers here and I think on every metric, they they missed the mark, uh, Ed unless you're seeing something different. I mean, in terms of around the world, when you look at um, you know, the the international scope of Netflix, I know they've put a lot more on the platform to try to get the international uh audience. I know for instance, you me being Greek, I was really excited to see, you know, Maestro in Blue come out because that was the first like Greek series, language series to hit the platform and I think its next season is going to be coming out soon. But is there some place around the world where Netflix is doing better than other places?

They they all uh manifest differently if they are to be judged by those financial metrics. And again, this is something the company's asked for, to be judged by those traditional financial metrics.

pages.title: Netflix Floundered by 20% This Year: One Analyst Says Its Streaming Monopoly WIll Net 88% Gains Within a Year - 24/7 Wall St.
pages.text:
Netflix Floundered by 20% This Year: One Analyst Says Its Streaming Monopoly WIll Net 88% Gains Within a Year
Netflix keeps posting double-digit revenue growth while its stock craters toward a 52-week low, and the gap between Wall Street's most bearish and most bullish analysts has rarely been this wide. Something has to give, and the next earnings report…
Published October 16, 2026, 7:15am ET · 4 min read
© hocus-focus / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) currently trades at $72.61, while Wall Street’s average 12-month price target is $92.06. That gap implies 26.8% upside.
Netflix is still the largest subscription streamer, with an audience approaching a billion people and revenue up 13.4% last quarter. The most optimistic analysts see much more. The Street-high target of $135 implies 85.9% upside.
Netflix keeps growing while its stock keeps falling. Investors have to decide which side is right: the market’s worry about engagement or the analysts’ confidence in pricing power.
A Walked-Away Deal and YouTube’s Living Room Grab Sent Netflix Into a 39% Slide
Netflix’s biggest problem is attention. HSBC noted that YouTube captured a record 14.2% share of US TV time, while Netflix’s own view hours grew just 2% in the first half of 2026. The stock is down 22.56% year to date and 39.66% over the past year. That one-year decline is a severe drop for a profitable mega-cap.
Strategy confusion made it worse. Netflix declined to match a higher bid for Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD) after calling the deal no longer attractive, and it collected a $2.80 billion termination fee. Earnings added pressure. First-quarter EPS of $1.23 missed the $1.345 estimate, and second-quarter free cash flow fell 32.73% to $1.53 billion on higher cash taxes.
Wall Street Trims Targets but Keeps the Buy Ratings
Recent revisions have been cuts to targets, while the ratings mostly held. Goldman Sachs reiterated Buy and lowered its target to $90, citing softer engagement and YouTube competition. Morgan Stanley also cut its target and still sees more than 40% upside. Wells Fargo issued a downgrade. Ratings still lean bullish: 7 analysts are most positive, 28 are positive, 15 are neutral and 1 are negative.
The bull case comes down to monetization. Netflix expects ad revenue to roughly double to about $3 billion, and its advertiser count grew 70% to more than 4,000 clients. Guidance calls for a 31.5% operating margin and roughly $12.5 billion in free cash flow. Netflix bought back $4.7 billion of stock last quarter, its largest buyback quarter ever, and still has $27.1 billion of authorization left.
The $135 case, associated with Pivotal Research and BofA Securities, argues that Netflix has won the global streaming wars outright. In that view, live sports and ad-tier growth bring in high-margin revenue. JPMorgan projects 24% annual EPS growth from 2025 through 2028. Consensus already expects EPS to rise from $3.5836 this year to $3.8087 next year. The first test is the upcoming earnings report, where management guided to $12.86 billion in revenue and $0.82 in EPS.
Disney and Roku Held Up While Netflix Fell Alone
This selloff is specific to Netflix. The rest of the streaming group has held steady or gained.
Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) is down just 1.96% year to date at $110.66. Its average target of $126.49 implies 14.3% upside. Analysts are firmly bullish, with 29 Strong Buy or Buy ratings against 3 Holds and 1 Sell, but the targets point to a smaller gain than Netflix’s.
Roku (NASDAQ:ROKU) is up 42.57% this year at $154.67, close to its $162.33 target, which implies only 4.95% upside. With 20 Holds against 7 Buy-side ratings, analysts see the rally as mostly priced in.
Netflix carries the biggest analyst-implied upside among these peers. Targets are estimates and can be wrong, but this gap reflects worries specific to Netflix more than a sector-wide correction.
Netflix Lags the S&P 500 While Trading at 19x Forward Earnings
At $72.61, Netflix sits 26.8% below its $92.06 consensus target. The stock is down 22.56% so far this year, and the S&P 500 is up 13.18%. Over one year, Netflix has fallen 39.66%, compared with a 16.03% gain for the index.
Shares trade near the bottom of their 52-week range of $65.08 to $124.86, at 19x forward earnings.
Ad Growth and Engagement Will Decide Whether Netflix Closes Its Target Gap
Optimism grows if ad revenue reaches roughly $3 billion and margins hold near 31.5%. That would show pricing power can offset slower viewing growth. Heavy buybacks at these prices would add to per-share gains if the stock moves toward the consensus target.
The bear case gains weight if YouTube keeps gaining TV share and Netflix’s engagement growth stalls. That would turn the low multiple into a value trap. If engagement keeps slipping, future price increases will be harder to push through, and the $135 case depends on those increases.
The stock trades at 19x forward earnings for a company growing revenue by double digits, a multiple that sits near the low end of its 52-week range. The consensus target looks more realistic than the Street high, and the upcoming earnings report should show which side has the better read.

Alex Sirois is a financial writer with experience spanning both retail and institutional investing. He has written for InvestorPlace and held roles at BNY Mellon and Bernstein, giving him a perspective that bridges Main Street portfolios and Wall Street analysis.
Alex holds an MBA from George Washington University and has built his career across multiple industries, including e-commerce, education, and translation — a breadth of experience that informs how he breaks down complex financial topics for everyday investors. His writing is conversational, actionable, and grounded in long-term, buy-and-hold investing principles.

Netflix Stock Drops After-Hours As Revenue Growth Slows Further And Q4 Sales Miss Expectations
The streaming giant projected its fourth consecutive quarter of slowing revenue growth amid advertising shortfalls and executive restructuring.
The Netflix logo is seen on the roof of an office building in Los Angeles, California, on May 29, 2026. (Photo by Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Netflix reported third-quarter revenue of $12.9 billion and earnings of $0.87 a share, topping Wall Street expectations of $0.82 per share.
Revenue growth is projected to drop to 12% in the fourth quarter (down from 17.6% last year).
Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters recently cut 6% of the workforce (~1,000 employees) and replaced Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria with veteran Disney executive Peter Rice.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Netflix Inc.(NFLX) on Tuesday reported third-quarter earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, but its shares fell 5% in after-hours trading after the streaming firm issued a soft revenue outlook for the fourth quarter, setting it up for the fourth consecutive period of decelerating sales growth.
The company reported $12.9 billion in third-quarter revenue, matching Wall Street forecasts, and its earnings at $0.87 a share topped expectations of $0.82 a share.
CRWV, NBIS, NVDA Jump Overnight: Musk Says SpaceX Could Rent Compute ‘Several Times Over,’ Analyst Dismisses Glut Fears
Despite the bottom-line beat, Netflix shares slipped as much as 7% in after-hours trading following the announcement.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Wall Street’s skepticism comes as the company works to reignite user engagement, scale its advertising layer, and adjust after failing to secure an acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery Inc.’s studio and streaming assets earlier this year.
Netflix has been struggling to consistently boost streaming revenue and new member additions over the past few quarters amid increasing competition from rival streaming services and is boosting programming of original content to ensure new additions.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Management Restructuring And Content Push
The earnings report follows a major operational overhaul led by Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters. Over the past week, Netflix announced a 6% workforce reduction—eliminating about 1,000 roles—its largest headcount cut since 2022.
In a bid to address perceived declines in programming quality and stagnant engagement, the company ousted Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin. To replace Bajaria, Netflix named Peter Rice, a seasoned industry executive who previously held leadership roles at both Walt Disney Co. and 21st Century Fox.
"With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical," Netflix stated in its letter to shareholders, acknowledging that while core priorities are being met, "we see room to do even better."
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, Netflix projects revenue of $13.4 billion, falling short of Wall Street estimates of $13.5 billion.
Netflix also projected a fourth-quarter operating margin of 26%, noting that severance and restructuring costs tied to its recent job cuts will weigh on profitability in the final three months of the year.

pages.title: The Gentlemen star announces exit from Netflix hit ahead of season 3
pages.text:
Entertainment:
The Gentlemen. L-R Joely Richardson as Lady Sabrina, Theo James as Eddie Horniman, Jasmine Blackborow as Charly Horniman, Chanel Cresswell as Tammy Horniman & Daniel Ings as Freddy Horniman | Christopher Rafael/Netflix
The Gentlemen might be coming back for a third season, but one of the show's original stars apparently will not be returning for season 3.
In a surprise turn of events, Daniel Ings has announced that he will not be returning for The Gentlemen season 3, exiting the series after two seasons. Ings casually broke the news in a new interview with HATC Magazine, confirming that he is not coming back for season 3, which is currently in production.
"I'm not in the next one. So that's a fun sense of closure. I kind of see it as closure for the character in a way; it just ends as this wild, broken, crazy, you know. I don't know, probably mumbling into the ether somewhere in the British countryside."
Interestingly, Ings did not specify why he will not be returning for The Gentlemen season 3, and the show did not hint at his departure in season 2. What seems to be the likely reason for his departure is Ings' busy schedule, as the actor has been highly sought after with several projects currently in various stages of development, including high-profile projects such as Star Wars: Starfighter.
We're going to have to see how Ings' character, Freddy Horniman, is written out of the series and whether the writing team decides to leave the door open for Freddy to return in future seasons or takes a more permanent approach to writing the character out.
Season 2 saw Freddy appear in a lessened role, but the ending suggested that Freddy would be back for season 3. The finale ended with Eddie confronting his brother for his betrayal and then forcing him into a van to kill his co-conspirator, which Freddy did, with the season ending with Freddy severing Dixon's head with a chainsaw. Could it be that Eddie decides to kill his brother after or simply sends him away? We're going to have to wait until season 3 arrives, but knowing that Ings won't be back certainly raises a lot of questions about where the writers will take the story next.
While Ings won't be back, we imagine they'll try to leave the door open for him to return, but with a show like The Gentlemen, there is really no telling what they might do. Every time we think we know where the show is going, it throws some new curveball our way, so there is no way of knowing what they might have planned for Freddy.
We'll certainly miss Ings in season 3, but we're excited to see what season 3 holds and to see who might be joining the cast for season 3. Little is known about the third season, including who will be back, with only series leads Theo James and Kaya Scodelario confirmed to return.
The Gentlemen is streaming now on Netflix.

Netflix hired Peter Rice as its new content chief as co-CEO Ted Sarandos tries to boost growth.
Frank Micelotta/Tubi via Getty Images; Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Chris Pizzello/AP
Netflix's third-quarter earnings failed to excite investors, a week after a major content executive shuffle and its biggest round of layoffs since 2022.
The streamer turned in results above expectations for the third quarter, but provided weak guidance for the rest of the year. Netflix said its earnings beat was primarily due to the timing of expenses.
Netflix's revenue growth slowed for a third straight quarter, and the company projected it would continue to decelerate in the fourth quarter.
Shares fell up to 6% in after-hours trading on Tuesday.
"While Netflix is growing, the pace of that growth is slowing," Forrester's Mike Proulx said. "That's a wake-up call for the company that once defined the streaming market and is now in need of growth reacceleration."
Here's how the streaming giant's Q3 financial results compared to the company's forecast:
Revenue: $12.87 billion vs $12.86 billion estimated ($11.5 billion in Q3 2025)
Earnings: $0.87 per share vs $0.82 per share estimated ($0.59 per share in Q3 2025)
Netflix told investors to expect earnings of $0.67 per share in the fourth quarter, below Wall Street's $0.73 per share estimate. The company's $13.44 billion revenue projection for Q4 was also lower than analysts' estimate of $13.51 billion.
The streaming leader cut its annual advertising forecast from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of its ad products.

"With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it's concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business," said analyst Ross Benes of Emarketer, Business Insider's sister company.
Heading into Q3 earnings, Netflix's stock was down over 44% in the last year as investors worried about engagement growth and stiff competition from YouTube and other free streamers.
Netflix said in its third-quarter shareholder letter that it knows "there's some investor concern about our view hours growth" but added that engagement "remains healthy."
"We do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we're confident we'll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing" its strategy, the shareholder letter said.
The company has invested in video games and podcasts but didn't mention either in its letter, outside a disclosure section on "forward-looking statements."
Netflix's results came less than a week after it shook up its content leadership team and cut about 1,000 workers.
Content chief Bela Bajaria is leaving her role after more than three years, Netflix announced last week. The company said Monday that film chief Dan Lin is also out.
Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney exec who ran Disney's TV division, including ABC and FX. Netflix hasn't yet said who will replace Lin; Rice will oversee film in the meantime.
"It's our goal to go from very good to great," co-CEO Greg Peters said of Netflix's content slate on the company's earnings call.
The leadership changes come as Netflix battles slowing viewership growth. The streaming powerhouse generated 97 billion viewing hours in the first half of the year, which was up 2% year-over-year.
Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said at an industry event hosted by Bloomberg last month that Netflix was "not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster."
"Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge, but it is a worthwhile start," Benes said.
Netflix layoffs were across its product, tech, HR, and legal teams. Co-CEOs Sarandos and Peters said in a memo to staffers that the company was downsizing so it can be "disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources."
Other media companies have laid off employees in the last month. NBCUniversal cut a few hundred global streaming tech employees in early October, and Disney trimmed its tech and HR teams in late September.
In the second quarter, Netflix's results were roughly in line with analysts' expectations. The stock sank 8% after the report as Netflix said it would cut back on how frequently it shared viewership data.

Netflix fell 4% after hours as its revenue growth outlook weakened.
Netflix cut its 2026 ad revenue forecast to $2.7 billion.
1. Leadership changes and slowing viewing hours add to investor concerns.
Netflix shares NFLX fell around 4% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after the streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts’ expectations but forecast slower revenue growth for the fourth consecutive quarter.
The company reported revenue of $12.9 billion for the quarter, up 12% from a year earlier and in line with Wall Street expectations.
Earnings reached 87 cents per share, beating analysts’ estimates of 82 cents. Net income increased approximately 43.5% year over year to $3.66 billion.
However, Netflix forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, below analysts’ expectations.
The company also projected full-year 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion, representing 13% growth and slightly below the midpoint of its previous forecast range of 13% to 14%.
The outlook comes as Netflix faces questions about viewer engagement, advertising growth and the quality of its programming.
Netflix forecasts slower revenue growth as advertising disappoints
Netflix’s revenue growth has slowed from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of last year to a projected 11.5% in the final three months of 2026.
The company attributed the advertising shortfall partly to a slower-than-expected rollout of some products for advertisers.
Netflix now expects advertising revenue of $2.7 billion this year, compared with its previous projection of approximately $3 billion.
The company said subscription revenue growth had exceeded its expectations.
The company’s operating margin improved to 34.6% in the third quarter from 28.2% a year earlier.
Free cash flow also increased to $2.9 billion from $2.66 billion in the same period last year.
Despite these improvements, investors remain focused on Netflix’s ability to sustain growth.
The company said in its shareholder letter that it recognised investor concerns about viewing hours but remained confident it could accelerate growth in time spent watching its content.
Netflix is expanding into live sports, podcasts and video games while adding third-party film and television programming.
The company is also seeking to increase engagement as competition for viewers intensifies across streaming platforms and other digital entertainment services.
Leadership changes follow concerns over programming quality
Netflix has made significant changes to its workforce and leadership as it seeks to improve its content offering.
Over the past week, the company cut approximately 6% of its workforce, or around 1,000 positions, and removed Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin from their roles.
The company appointed Peter Rice, a veteran film and television executive who previously held senior positions at Walt Disney and 21st Century Fox, to replace Bajaria.
The changes follow growing concerns that Netflix has struggled to deliver major television and film hits capable of attracting widespread attention.
Its Emmy Awards haul fell to a 10-year low in 2026, while viewing activity has shown signs of slowing.
Netflix remains a leading global streaming platform, with more than 325 million subscribers.
However, ratings tracker Nielsen puts its share of US television viewing at 7.8%, compared with approximately 14% for YouTube.
According to figures cited by The Wall Street Journal, Netflix viewers watched only 2% more programming in the first half of 2026 than a year earlier.
Stock faces pressure as investors reassess growth prospects
Netflix shares have faced sustained pressure following the company’s unsuccessful bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery’s film and television studios and HBO Max.
The stock has fallen approximately 25% this year and more than 40% over the past year, according to the supplied reports.
Investor attention is increasingly centred on the company’s ability to increase viewing hours and generate growth without a major acquisition.
Netflix’s customer retention remains relatively strong. Research firm Antenna estimated that its subscription churn rate was around 2% in September, unchanged from August and the lowest in the industry.
The company also said customer responses to price increases this year were in line with expectations, indicating that engagement remained healthy.
Nevertheless, the weaker advertising outlook and slowing revenue growth have added to concerns about its near-term performance.
Netflix’s improving margins and cash flow provide some support, but investors will be watching whether its content strategy and new entertainment offerings can translate into stronger viewing activity and sustained growth.
