Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement, revenue growth
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:41 PM CDT 3 min read
California-based streaming giant Netflix saw shares drop amid concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth (JUSTIN SULLIVAN)
Netflix stock dropped more than five percent Tuesday afternoon after its quarterly earnings release failed to assuage investor concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how the company measures engagement, and added that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.
The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streamers, gaming and sports.
Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months" and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes," John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.
In its third quarter ending in September, Netflix recorded $12.87 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.
It did not provide overall figures for subscriber view hours in the quarter, but noted that in India the metric increased 24 percent compared to the same period last year.
In July, Netflix said subscribers spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a 2 percent increase over the first half of 2025.
It stopped reporting subscriber numbers in the first half of 2025.
But the company touted growth outside the US while acknowledging challenges stateside.
"We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working," co-CEO Ted Sarandos told investors on an analyst call Tuesday, highlighting engagement, subscribers, revenue and profits across Latin America, Europe and Asia.
"The U.S. is also working. It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," Sarandos continued.
The company will also reportedly cut around 6 percent of its workforce, or 1,000 jobs, according to media reports.
Among them were seven high-level employees in charge of television deals and content, the Hollywood Reporter reported last week.
The company also recently replaced chief content officer Bela Bajaria, who oversaw popular shows including "Stranger Things," "Bridgerton," and "Squid Game," in addition to pushing the company's live entertainment strategy, according to CNBC.
Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice to be its new content chief.
"Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work," Sarandos said on the call Tuesday.
Competition from other streamers has forced Netflix to work harder to attract and retain both paid and ad-supported members.
The company has increasingly dipped into live sports -- with agreements to stream major events like the Olympics and World Cup -- in addition to gaming and shorter-form content. The NFL and WWE are also on board to stream live events.
In the US, it reached 7.8 percent of streaming television viewers in July compared to YouTube's 14.2 percent, a record for the Google-owned site, according to media analytics firm Nielsen.
The World Cup lifted overall television viewership in July, according to Nielsen.
"It's really important to remember, roughly 95 percent of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core, where we see a long runway for future growth," Sarandos said on Tuesday's call, emphasizing its commitment to traditional television and film content.
The company also missed expectations on advertising revenue growth.
"We are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing" on advertising, nonetheless, co-CEO Greg Peters said on the call.
"We see the benefits when we continue to roll out other products like new ad formats, which help with our growth," Peters added.

Netflix (NFLX -1.66%) released third-quarter earnings after hours on Tuesday, and it was another disappointment for investors. The stock was trading down 6% after hours.
While its headline numbers were slightly ahead of expectations, Netflix's engagement remained weak, and its trend of slowing growth continued. In fact, the company reported its slowest top-line growth in three years, and it expects it to continue to moderate in the fourth quarter.
Overall revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, which matched expectations, while its operating margin came in at 34% due to the timing of its content spend. On the bottom line, earnings per share improved from $0.59 to $0.87, beating estimates of $0.82.
However, beyond the existing concerns about engagement and its weak original content slate, one number underscored Netflix's troubles. The company cut its ad revenue guidance for the year from $3 billion to $2.7 billion, indicating weakness in what's supposed to be a key growth market for the streamer.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
Netflix was late to launch its advertising business, finally pulling the trigger in 2022 after years of resistance. The decision has turned out to be a success, giving customers a lower-priced option and allowing advertisers to meet audiences where they are, on streaming. The two-tiered advertising model has become the norm in the streaming industry, and all of Netflix's rivals offer some version of a higher-priced ad-free tier and a lower-priced tier with ads.
Advertising was also supposed to give Netflix an avenue for growth at a time when its subscription business is believed to be maturing, especially in core markets like the U.S. Netflix no longer reports quarterly subscriber numbers, so investors don't have much insight into subscriber growth anymore.
Netflix cut its ad revenue forecast due to a "slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities," which places the blame for the shortfall on a technical issue rather than a business issue like weak demand from advertisers or poor engagement. That's a good sign for investors, but still a disappointment, nonetheless.
Is it a red flag?
Advertising still makes up a small fraction of Netflix's revenue. The streamer expects to bring in $51.1 billion in revenue this year, meaning that advertising makes up less than 6% of its revenue. The subscription business still dominates.
However, advertising is a key part of the growth story, and it could face increased scrutiny from Wall Street, especially given the disappointing engagement trends.
The advertising weakness isn't a red flag, but Netflix has become a "show-me story" this year, meaning it needs to prove to investors that it can stop its growth slowdown and improve engagement, or it will continue to face skepticism, which is likely to push the stock lower. The advertising weakness, whether it's due to a one-off technical issue or something else, only adds to those concerns.

Netflix won the fewest Emmy Awards in a decade this year, and the company isn’t growing fast enough, according to Co-Chief Executive Officer Ted Sarandos.
“The content’s getting very expensive, and there’s just still too many players,” said Ken Mahoney of Mahoney Asset Management. “I think there’s so many better tech stories out there than Netflix that have sticky customers.”
Netflix is taking steps to improve its content and raise its audience numbers. On Monday, it announced that the head of its film division, Dan Lin, was leaving, and last week replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with Peter Rice, the former chairman of Walt Disney Television. The company also plans to cut about 1,000 positions in various departments globally in a bid to reduce costs.
For investors, however, the issue is this earnings report won’t reflect those moves. And even if executives give a solid revenue outlook, it’s unlikely to quell the debate around engagement, according to Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Geetha Raganathan.
“A stronger 4Q slate could revive viewing and ads, but investors will want proof that engagement can improve without derailing margin expansion,” she wrote in an Oct. 19 note. The addition of Rice signals a potential pivot toward “more premium, conversation-driving originals and higher 2027 content spending,” she added.
Analysts following the company expect it to report a 12% rise in revenue in the third quarter to $12.9 billion, and a 39% jump in earnings to 82 cents a share, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Its gross margin is expected to be 51%, down slightly from the second quarter.
Wall Street remains generally bullish on the stock, with an average price target of about $92 suggesting a more than 30% rise over the next 12 months. And while sentiment has weakened, with two analysts putting sell-equivalent ratings on the shares in the last month, bulls see a vibe shift coming.
“While total viewing is still weak, quality has improved as reflected in hour/top-10 title and the number of sequels is increasing” through the end of the year, Oppenheimer analysts led by Jason Helfstein wrote in an Oct. 14 note. Three months of US price increases and one month of higher ad rates should give revenue a boost, and the recent headcount reductions will allow for more spending on marketing or content or provide upside to margins, they added.
Management may offer some indications for what it expects in 2027, but the company is unlikely to offer thorough guidance, according to Mark Mahaney of Evercore ISI. He was particularly enthusiastic about Netflix’s recent release of East of Eden.
“East of Eden looks very promising to us,” Mahaney wrote in a note to clients on Oct. 16. “Steinbeck is BACK!”
Ad revenue may be more important to investors than audience engagement, according to Wedbush’s Alicia Reese, who says the segment is on track to double to roughly $3 billion in 2026.
“Netflix is actively making changes that should address both its engagement issues and shift dollars from heavy infrastructure to more focused content spend,” Reese wrote in an Oct. 16 note.
One argument for buying the stock would be valuation, considering it’s priced at less than 19 times earnings projected over the next 12 months, the lowest valuation since 2022 and a steep discount to its 10-year average of 49.
That helps explain why KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst Justin Patterson believes the Netflix bear case is already priced into the share price.
“The bear case on slowing engagement and more modest margin expansion is arguably priced in,” he wrote in an Oct. 12 note. “We believe management is aware of these issues, and expect to see corrective action taken across content investment and expense realignment to bolster growth and earnings, and deliver value.”

Dan Lin is out as Netflix‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter.

Lin joined Netflix in 2024, taking over from then film chief Scott Stuber. Under Stuber, Netflix became known as the place where name filmmakers could land big budgets and paydays as the traditional studios implemented more cost-conscious spending practices. During this time, the streamer consistently ended up with best picture nominations, but top awards have notoriously evaded Netflix films.
Lin, who was hired by Bajaria, was brought in to curb spending while (ideally) increasing the quality of the entire film slate, not just the titles from big-name directors.
Under Lin, the streamer‘s movies division was reorganized by genre, with deputies like Kira Goldberg, Ori Marmur and Jason Young handling films that fell under categories like sci-fi, rom-com and family film. Netflix began offering more mid-size films that have been ignored by theatrical players, including big book adaptations like Remarkably Bright Creatures and People We Meet on Vacation, as well as mid-budget action films like Apex and The RIP.
(This is not to say that Netflix’s Lin tenure was without big swings — see: Greta Gerwig‘s Narnia movie due out next year or David Fincher’s The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth— but the offerings no doubt slowed.)
Lin came from his production company Rideback, which minted the $1 billion grossing Aladdin and was involved in the hit It movies as well as The Lego Movies. He departed the company when he joined Netflix, leaving partners at the helm who found another $1 billion hit with last summer’s live-action Lilo & Stitch. Presumably, he could return to Rideback now that his Netflix tenure is up.

In 2027, Netflix will start manage its consumer products licensing business in Brazil directly, working side by side with partner brands. To support this new chapter, the local team will include specialists in creative development and integrated projects to support Netflix’s stories and fandoms with brands’ expertise in products, categories and retail to deliver products and experiences.
After establishing the business through a commercial representation model, which was instrumental in building its presence in Brazil, Netflix will work more closely with licensees through a larger local team dedicated to faster decision-making, with a focus on relevance, engagement and innovation.
In practice, direct relationships will evolve the way products are developed. Partners will be able to tell Netflix directly which audiences, categories or cultural conversations they want to explore. Netflix, in turn, will identify opportunities through its knowledge of fandoms: the most talked-about characters, what went viral in the previous season and what fans want more of.

Streaming major trims 2026 ad revenue forecast to $2.7 billion as slower growth and US content execution weigh on investor sentiment, viewing hours rise 24% in India
Published:
Netflix reported a 44% year-on-year increase in third-quarter profit and an 11.8% rise in revenue, marking the lowest growth rate in three years, but issued a weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook, leading to a nearly 6% drop in shares.
The company lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to approximately $2.7 billion, citing delays in product rollouts and partner integrations, despite expecting over 80% growth in its advertising business this year.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos emphasized the need for better execution in the U.S. market and highlighted the importance of producing quality content to enhance subscriber engagement amid increasing competition from platforms like YouTube and TikTok.
Netflix experienced a 24% increase in viewing hours in India during the third quarter, driven by successful local content, and reported its largest quarter of paid net additions in the region.
Netflix’s third-quarter profit rose 44% year-on-year and revenue jumped 11.8% (lowest rate of increase in 3 years), but its weaker-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings outlook and a reduction in its full-year advertising revenue forecast triggered a fresh sell-off in its shares on Tuesday, highlighting the pressure to sustain growth as it scales up its advertising business.
Netflix reduced its advertising forecast for 2026 to roughly $2.7 billion, down from about $3 billion. Some ad product capabilities rolled out slightly slower than expected, executives said in their quarterly letter to shareholders.
Shares fell nearly 6% to $64.66 in after-hours trading on October 20. The stock had already lost more than 25% of its value over the preceding year, reflecting concerns about engagement growth, competition and the sustainability of its premium valuation.
"I know that we could do better," Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said in a post-earnings video call. "Now we've seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level."
Third-quarter revenue rose 11.8% to $12.87 billion, in line with Wall Street forecasts, but the lowest rate of increase in nearly ⁠three years. The company forecast fourth-quarter net income of $2.79 billion and EPS of 67 cents, below the average analyst forecast of $3.07 billion and 73 cents.
Sarandos said the company plans to focus on its core business of producing quality TV shows and movies to make Netflix a must-have service, and the recent executive shakeup was a step toward that goal. In its earnings report, Netflix said it would continue to expand its offerings through licensing more third-party ‌content.
Netflix expects fourth-quarter revenue of $13.44 billion, up 11.5% year-on-year, but forecasts net income of $2.79 billion and earnings per share of 67 cents. Both figures fall short of analysts’ expectations of $3.07 billion and 73 cents, respectively. The company also projects an operating margin of 26%, down from 34.6% in Q3.
For the full year, Netflix maintained its revenue guidance of $51.1 billion, representing approximately 13% growth, and an operating margin target of 31.5%. However, it lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast to approximately $2.7 billion from $3 billion, citing delays in rolling out advertising products and partner integrations. Despite the revision, the advertising business is expected to grow more than 80% this year, according to co-CEO Greg Peters.
For advertisers and media buyers, the revision highlights the difference between growing demand for streaming inventory and building the technology, partnerships and formats needed to monetise it at scale.
Sarandos calls for stronger US content execution
Sarandos said Netflix’s underlying strategy remained unchanged, centred on exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events, supported by licensing and global distribution.
“Our business and our business flywheel are working. There’s no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S.,” Sarandos said.
Notably, Netflix has posted monthly subscriber losses in the US throughout 2026, with no net additions reported ⁠for any month up to September, data from analytics firm Antenna showed, as reported by Reuters. Antenna tracks US subscription purchases via sources like credit card transactions, but excludes subscriptions acquired through wholesale bundles.
Sarandos acknowledged that the company had delivered “some really solid doubles and triples this year”, but said it needed more breakout hits that could travel internationally. “I know that we could do better,” he added, pointing to an opportunity to take the content slate to the next level.
Sarandos also highlighted the importance of creative talent, saying incoming chief content officer Peter Rice understood talent relations in a competitive market. Netflix recently laid off around 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and announced leadership changes involving content chief Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin.
Live sports and events remain central to the growth strategy. Sarandos said such programming can attract new members, support advertising revenue and increase value for existing subscribers. Yet competition from YouTube and TikTok, alongside questions over viewing-hour growth, puts greater pressure on Netflix to deliver stronger engagement.
The challenge now is to convert its global reach and content investments into faster growth, while improving advertising monetisation and maintaining profitability.
India is the example Netflix chose. View hours there grew 24% year over year in the third quarter, led by Lock Upp, its first daily reality series, according to the letter. Netflix recorded its largest quarter of paid net additions in India, and revenue there grew about 18% on a currency-neutral basis.

Key Risk: Ad growth fails to translate into meaningful revenue acceleration, so overall growth keeps slowing and the stock de-rates.

Netflix shares are down about 25% in 2026 as investors await Q3 results.
Q3 revenue guidance implies a deceleration to about 11.7%.
Investors will watch Q4 guidance and operating margins.
Netflix is set to report its third-quarter 2026 results after Tuesday's market close, with investors looking for signs that advertising growth and improving profitability can offset slowing revenue growth and intensifying competition from YouTube.
The streaming giant's shares have fallen approximately 23% year to date, raising the stakes for its latest earnings report as analysts reassess its growth prospects and valuation.
Attention will centre on quarterly revenue, operating margins, advertising monetisation and management's outlook for the final three months of the year.
Analysts expect Netflix to report revenue of $12.87 billion, an increase of 11.8% from a year earlier.
Revenue growth slowdown puts Q4 outlook in focus
Netflix reported revenue of $12.56 billion in the second quarter, up 13.4% year over year, while diluted earnings per share of $0.80 edged past the consensus estimate of $0.79.
For the third quarter, management guided for revenue of approximately $12.86 billion and earnings per share of $0.82, below previous Wall Street expectations.
The outlook triggered a sell-off after the company's previous results.
Revenue growth has slowed over recent quarters, falling from 17.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 16.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and 13.4% in the second quarter.
The third-quarter revenue guidance implies further deceleration to about 11.7%.
"Overall, we're not growing as fast as I want us to," co-CEO Ted Sarandos said recently at Bloomberg's 2026 Screentime event in Los Angeles.
"We are, though, also doing things that create a lot of headwind to that number," he added.
Investors will thus assess whether the company can stabilise growth or whether its expansion is slowing faster than anticipated.
The fourth-quarter outlook could prove particularly important.
Netflix's full-year 2026 revenue guidance stands at $51 billion to $51.4 billion.
Advertising growth offers a potential boost
Advertising remains a key part of Netflix's strategy to diversify revenue beyond subscriptions.
The company expects its advertising business to generate approximately $3 billion in 2026, roughly double the previous year's figure.
Even so, advertising would account for only about 6% of annual sales.
Netflix has taken several steps to expand its advertising platform.
It concluded its 2026 US upfront advertising negotiations in August with commitments nearly doubling, secured its first Media Rating Council accreditation for Netflix Ads Suite and made Pause Ads available programmatically across major demand-side platforms, according to Zacks.
Investors will look for evidence that these initiatives are translating into sustained revenue growth and improving monetisation.
Jefferies maintained its Buy rating on Netflix last week, with an $85 price target, arguing that the company has significant room to expand monetisation, margins and share repurchases.
Analyst Brent Thill expects annual revenue growth of 11% between 2026 and 2029, driven by subscriber additions, price increases and advertising.
Jefferies forecasts advertising revenue rising to $7.5 billion by 2029 from $3 billion in 2026.
Thill also sees scope for further subscription price increases.
Netflix's standard plan costs about 60% less than competing services on a price-per-viewing-hour basis in the US, he noted, potentially giving the company room to raise prices.
Margin expansion remains central to the investment case
While revenue growth has slowed, Netflix's operating margins have continued to improve.
The company reported a 33.4% operating margin in the second quarter and guided for 33.2% in the third quarter.
Its full-year operating margin target stands at 31.5%, and investors will watch for any changes to that forecast.
Morningstar senior equity analyst Matthew Dolgin has identified margin expansion as a key component of the investment case.
"Ongoing margin expansion is a key component of the thesis behind investing in Netflix," Dolgin said.
The company's ability to control content costs while growing advertising revenue could help sustain profitability even as sales growth moderates.
Jefferies forecasts approximately 190 basis points of annual operating margin expansion through 2029.
Thill also expects more than $50 billion in cumulative free cash flow over three years, potentially providing substantial capacity for share repurchases.
Some analysts have sought to highlight Netflix's international opportunity amid slowing growth.
Morningstar expects Netflix to deliver a compound annual revenue growth rate of about 10% through 2030, followed by mid-single-digit growth in the latter five years of its 10-year forecast.
"We expect international markets to lead this growth, given the opportunities they still have to add new members," Dolgin wrote.
Deutsche Bank recently upgraded the stock to Buy from Hold, even though it lowered its PT to $95 from $100, with analyst Bryan Kraft noting that international engagement has increased year over year in each of the past four six-month periods.
Kraft believes Netflix's global scale, brand and production capabilities could support a broader "Netflix As A Platform" opportunity over time.
Growth across Netflix's four reported geographic regions will therefore be another important metric, particularly as international markets account for much of the remaining subscriber expansion opportunity.
Management changes and analyst downgrades add pressure
Netflix is also undergoing organisational changes.
Last week, the company announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice would become chief content officer, overseeing its global content organisation, including scripted and unscripted series, films and live events.
He will replace 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team, including its live sports strategy.
The company also announced plans on October 14 to cut approximately 1,000 jobs, or about 6% of its workforce, increasing scrutiny of cost discipline as content spending remains significant.
Recent analyst actions have reflected divided views on the stock.
Wells Fargo downgraded Netflix to Underweight in September, citing the possibility of declining viewing hours for its leading original programmes.
HSBC lowered its rating to Hold from Buy and cut its price target to $76.
Deutsche Bank subsequently upgraded the stock to Buy with a $95 target, while Goldman Sachs maintained its Buy rating with a $90 target.
KeyBanc, Morgan Stanley, Barclays and Huber Research have also lowered their price targets this month.
For Netflix, Tuesday's results will test whether advertising growth and margin expansion can offset slowing sales and heightened competition.
Investors will also look for signs that the company's international growth, pricing power and cash generation can sustain earnings expansion over the coming years.

Netflix keeps posting double-digit revenue growth while its stock craters toward a 52-week low, and the gap between Wall Street's most bearish and most bullish analysts has rarely been this wide. Something has to give, and the next earnings report…
Published October 16, 2026, 7:15am ET · 4 min read

Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) currently trades at $72.61, while Wall Street’s average 12-month price target is $92.06. That gap implies 26.8% upside.
Netflix is still the largest subscription streamer, with an audience approaching a billion people and revenue up 13.4% last quarter. The most optimistic analysts see much more. The Street-high target of $135 implies 85.9% upside.
Netflix keeps growing while its stock keeps falling. Investors have to decide which side is right: the market’s worry about engagement or the analysts’ confidence in pricing power.
A Walked-Away Deal and YouTube’s Living Room Grab Sent Netflix Into a 39% Slide
Netflix’s biggest problem is attention. HSBC noted that YouTube captured a record 14.2% share of US TV time, while Netflix’s own view hours grew just 2% in the first half of 2026. The stock is down 22.56% year to date and 39.66% over the past year. That one-year decline is a severe drop for a profitable mega-cap.
Strategy confusion made it worse. Netflix declined to match a higher bid for Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD) after calling the deal no longer attractive, and it collected a $2.80 billion termination fee. Earnings added pressure. First-quarter EPS of $1.23 missed the $1.345 estimate, and second-quarter free cash flow fell 32.73% to $1.53 billion on higher cash taxes.
Wall Street Trims Targets but Keeps the Buy Ratings
Recent revisions have been cuts to targets, while the ratings mostly held. Goldman Sachs reiterated Buy and lowered its target to $90, citing softer engagement and YouTube competition. Morgan Stanley also cut its target and still sees more than 40% upside. Wells Fargo issued a downgrade. Ratings still lean bullish: 7 analysts are most positive, 28 are positive, 15 are neutral and 1 are negative.
The bull case comes down to monetization. Netflix expects ad revenue to roughly double to about $3 billion, and its advertiser count grew 70% to more than 4,000 clients. Guidance calls for a 31.5% operating margin and roughly $12.5 billion in free cash flow. Netflix bought back $4.7 billion of stock last quarter, its largest buyback quarter ever, and still has $27.1 billion of authorization left.
The $135 case, associated with Pivotal Research and BofA Securities, argues that Netflix has won the global streaming wars outright. In that view, live sports and ad-tier growth bring in high-margin revenue. JPMorgan projects 24% annual EPS growth from 2025 through 2028. Consensus already expects EPS to rise from $3.5836 this year to $3.8087 next year. The first test is the upcoming earnings report, where management guided to $12.86 billion in revenue and $0.82 in EPS.
Disney and Roku Held Up While Netflix Fell Alone
This selloff is specific to Netflix. The rest of the streaming group has held steady or gained.
Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) is down just 1.96% year to date at $110.66. Its average target of $126.49 implies 14.3% upside. Analysts are firmly bullish, with 29 Strong Buy or Buy ratings against 3 Holds and 1 Sell, but the targets point to a smaller gain than Netflix’s.
Roku (NASDAQ:ROKU) is up 42.57% this year at $154.67, close to its $162.33 target, which implies only 4.95% upside. With 20 Holds against 7 Buy-side ratings, analysts see the rally as mostly priced in.
Netflix carries the biggest analyst-implied upside among these peers. Targets are estimates and can be wrong, but this gap reflects worries specific to Netflix more than a sector-wide correction.
Netflix Lags the S&P 500 While Trading at 19x Forward Earnings
At $72.61, Netflix sits 26.8% below its $92.06 consensus target. The stock is down 22.56% so far this year, and the S&P 500 is up 13.18%. Over one year, Netflix has fallen 39.66%, compared with a 16.03% gain for the index.
Shares trade near the bottom of their 52-week range of $65.08 to $124.86, at 19x forward earnings.
Ad Growth and Engagement Will Decide Whether Netflix Closes Its Target Gap
Optimism grows if ad revenue reaches roughly $3 billion and margins hold near 31.5%. That would show pricing power can offset slower viewing growth. Heavy buybacks at these prices would add to per-share gains if the stock moves toward the consensus target.
The bear case gains weight if YouTube keeps gaining TV share and Netflix’s engagement growth stalls. That would turn the low multiple into a value trap. If engagement keeps slipping, future price increases will be harder to push through, and the $135 case depends on those increases.
The stock trades at 19x forward earnings for a company growing revenue by double digits, a multiple that sits near the low end of its 52-week range. The consensus target looks more realistic than the Street high, and the upcoming earnings report should show which side has the better read.

The Gentlemen might be coming back for a third season, but one of the show's original stars apparently will not be returning for season 3.
In a surprise turn of events, Daniel Ings has announced that he will not be returning for The Gentlemen season 3, exiting the series after two seasons. Ings casually broke the news in a new interview with HATC Magazine, confirming that he is not coming back for season 3, which is currently in production.
"I'm not in the next one. So that's a fun sense of closure. I kind of see it as closure for the character in a way; it just ends as this wild, broken, crazy, you know. I don't know, probably mumbling into the ether somewhere in the British countryside."
Interestingly, Ings did not specify why he will not be returning for The Gentlemen season 3, and the show did not hint at his departure in season 2. What seems to be the likely reason for his departure is Ings' busy schedule, as the actor has been highly sought after with several projects currently in various stages of development, including high-profile projects such as Star Wars: Starfighter.
We're going to have to see how Ings' character, Freddy Horniman, is written out of the series and whether the writing team decides to leave the door open for Freddy to return in future seasons or takes a more permanent approach to writing the character out.
Season 2 saw Freddy appear in a lessened role, but the ending suggested that Freddy would be back for season 3. The finale ended with Eddie confronting his brother for his betrayal and then forcing him into a van to kill his co-conspirator, which Freddy did, with the season ending with Freddy severing Dixon's head with a chainsaw. Could it be that Eddie decides to kill his brother after or simply sends him away? We're going to have to wait until season 3 arrives, but knowing that Ings won't be back certainly raises a lot of questions about where the writers will take the story next.
While Ings won't be back, we imagine they'll try to leave the door open for him to return, but with a show like The Gentlemen, there is really no telling what they might do. Every time we think we know where the show is going, it throws some new curveball our way, so there is no way of knowing what they might have planned for Freddy.
We'll certainly miss Ings in season 3, but we're excited to see what season 3 holds and to see who might be joining the cast for season 3. Little is known about the third season, including who will be back, with only series leads Theo James and Kaya Scodelario confirmed to return.

Netflix shares drop on slowing engagement, revenue growth
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:41 PM CDT 3 min read
California-based streaming giant Netflix saw shares drop amid concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth (JUSTIN SULLIVAN)
Netflix stock dropped more than five percent Tuesday afternoon after its quarterly earnings release failed to assuage investor concerns about a slowdown in viewer engagement and revenue growth.
"We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the company said in a letter to investors, referring to how the company measures engagement, and added that it was "confident" it could accelerate that growth.
The California-based streaming giant has struggled to meet investor expectations for several quarters as it faces competition from other streamers, gaming and sports.
Netflix "has underperformed significantly over the last 6-12 months" and investors are concerned "about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes," John Belton, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, told AFP in a statement.
In its third quarter ending in September, Netflix recorded $12.87 billion in revenue and $3.7 billion in net income, above investor expectations, according to FactSet.
It did not provide overall figures for subscriber view hours in the quarter, but noted that in India the metric increased 24 percent compared to the same period last year.
In July, Netflix said subscribers spent 97 billion hours watching content in the first half of the year, a 2 percent increase over the first half of 2025.

•We delivered our Q3 forecast and expect to deliver on our full year 2026 guidance.
◦Q3 revenue grew 12% year over year (11% on a F/X neutral basis1) to $12.9B, consistent with our forecast. Operating margin was 34.6%, up from 28.2% in Q3’25 and ahead of our forecast primarily due to the timing of expenses.
◦For 2026, we expect revenue of $51.1B (+13% year over year) and an operating margin of 31.5%.
•The core of our service is delivering differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events. Q3 highlights include The Last House, Facing El Chapo, Death of the Pastor’s Wife, our NFL Game from Melbourne, and a very successful slate in India.
•We’ll continue to expand our entertainment offering through licensing and new ways to bring more third-party content to our service, like our TF1 partnership in France. Our audience, which is approaching one billion people, and our best-in-class product capabilities, make us great partners for studios, networks and creative talent.
•Member response to our 2026 price changes is consistent with prior adjustments and our expectations, an indicator that our engagement - which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing - remains healthy and that we continue to deliver strong value to members.
•We’ll close out 2026 with an exciting slate including The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, limited series The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey, starring Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen, new seasons of The Diplomat, Nobody Wants This and Lupin, the series finale of Emily in Paris, three NFL games on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day, and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight.
Our summary results, and forecast for Q4, are below.

Revenue in Q3 grew 12% year over year (+11% on a foreign exchange (F/X) neutral basis), and was in-line with our forecast. In Q3, revenue growth was driven primarily by subscription revenue, reflecting increases in memberships and pricing, growth in advertising revenue and a favorable impact from F/X rates, net of hedging. Membership growth benefited from continued, healthy retention in every region; globally and in the US, churn improved year-over-year and was better than forecast.
Q3’26 operating income totaled $4.5B (+37% year over year) and operating margin of 34.6% was up versus 28.2% in Q3’25. Both Q3 operating income and margin were ahead of forecast due primarily to the timing of expenses and the slight upside in revenue. As a result, diluted EPS for the quarter amounted to $0.87 vs. $0.59 in Q3’25 (+49% year over year).
As a reminder, the guidance we provide is our actual internal forecast at the time we report and we strive for accuracy. Our primary financial metrics are revenue for growth and operating margin for profitability. Our goal is to sustain healthy revenue growth, expand operating profit and margin, and deliver growing free cash flow.
In Q4, we expect revenue of $13.4 billion, which represents year over year growth of 12% (or 11% F/X neutral) driven by growth in memberships, pricing, and ad revenue. We project a Q4 operating margin of 26.0% which includes ~120 basis points negative impact associated with our recently announced headcount reductions, and compares with 24.5% in the year ago quarter. These organizational changes enable us to continue to aggressively invest in high impact areas to improve our service, and drive growth and innovation.
Our guidance for Q4 means that for the full year 2026 we expect revenue of $51.1B, or growth of 13% (+12% on a F/X neutral basis). This is 0.2% below the mid-point of our prior 2026 revenue forecast range - while subscription revenue growth has outperformed our expectations, we currently expect 2026 ad revenue of ~$2.7B vs. approximately $3B previously (due to slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities). We anticipate an operating margin of 31.5% for 2026 (31.4% based on F/X rates as of January 1, 2026) vs. 29.5% in 2025. Our updated 2026 margin guidance includes ~30 basis points negative impact associated with our Q4 headcount reductions. Our forecast implies annual operating income growth of 20%+ for 2026.
Our mission is to entertain the world while building a wildly successful business. Our strategy is simple: invest in differentiated, exclusive, professionally-produced entertainment like Netflix originals that spark conversation, bring in more members, and make us a “must-have” service. We pair these originals, which anchor our service, with a broad, complementary selection of third-party programming, a great discovery experience, and leading global distribution. Together, this fuels engagement (quality, quantity, and variety of viewing) and, in turn, revenue and profit. The core of our service is streaming TV, film and live events, monetized via subscription and advertising. It represents the vast majority of our spending and nearly all of our revenue, and is the engine of our business for which we see a long runway of growth.
To successfully execute this strategy, we focus on three priorities: 1) delivering more entertainment value to our members, 2) leveraging technology to improve all aspects of our service, and 3) improving our monetization. These priorities work in concert to drive acquisition and retention, create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand. We reinvest returns in our business so we can win more moments of truth and fund the next wave of entertainment. Done well,
this makes our service the one where members go first to look for entertainment and the last service they would cancel, with industry-leading retention and continued member and ARM2 growth.
With intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention, strategic clarity and excellent execution are critical. In Q3, we delivered well across all three priorities, but we see room to do even better with focused, continuous improvement.
In Q3, we had a variety of hits from around the world that members loved. Plastic Beauty* (12M views3) is on track to be our most-viewed series ever in Japan; The Secret Woman* (47M) is trending to be our most-viewed Danish title ever; Facing El Chapo* (58M) is pacing to be our second most-viewed Mexican title globally; and The Perfect Lie* (17M) is on track to become our most-viewed series out of the Netherlands. Non-English viewing has grown from under 10% of total viewing a decade ago to more than a third today. These hits reflect our decade-long commitment to creating content around the world that resonates locally, and has the potential to travel globally.
Other successful Q3 titles include:
•UCAN: Death of the Pastor's Wife* (45M), The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare* (38M), My Life With The Walter Boys S3* (29M), Little House on the Prairie (29M), The Last House* (91M) and Why Did I Get Married Again* (36M)
•EMEA: The Gentlemen S2* (33M) and A Toxic Love Story* (43M) from the UK, Elite Force* (25M) from France, Blood Sacrifice* (23M) from Sweden
•LATAM: My Daughter's Father* (23M) from Mexico and Nando Between Two Worlds - A Sintonia Film* (18M) from Brazil
•APAC: The East Palace (21M) and Our Sticky Love* (22M) from Korea
Complementing our Netflix originals, we continue to expand our entertainment offering through licensing and bringing more third-party content to our service in new ways. Our broad distribution (we’re serving an audience approaching one billion people) and industry leading monetization make us great partners for studios, networks and creative talent. For example, we partnered with Take-Two to unveil a sneak peek of the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI5 in August. And we recently secured a new licensing deal with Disney6 which brings a variety of current and library series and films to our service for our members to enjoy, including all five Ice Age films which reached our global weekly Top 10 list and are building consumer awareness in advance of Disney’s theatrical release of Ice Age: Boiling Point in February 2027.
2 Average revenue per membership.
3 A view is defined as hours viewed divided by runtime for each title. Our investment in our product capabilities, including our new TV UI, enables us to seamlessly integrate and merchandise more third party content to Netflix members. This summer we launched our partnership with TF1, a leading French broadcaster. This partnership enables us to provide our French members with even more highly local series, film, news and sports programming, all within a frictionless choosing and viewing experience that complements our French slate and global programming. We’re pleased with the TF1 partnership and the early metrics indicate that it’s generating incremental viewing in France.
We also continue to invest in our ad tech stack (Netflix Ads Suite). In Q3, we extended programmatic access through globally-available CTV marketplace deals, and secured new partnerships with MercadoLibre in LATAM and AdForm in EMEA. We are also expanding capabilities to in-DSP measurement including reach, frequency, and attribution. Also, we will introduce our advertising tier to 15 new countries in 2027. The first tranche of new market launches will happen in March 2027: nine countries in EMEA7, Colombia, Peru and New Zealand (a new addition from our previous announcement).
We know there’s some investor concern about our view hours growth. Member response to our 2026 price increases is consistent with prior price changes and our expectations, an indicator that our engagement - which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing - remains healthy and that we continue to deliver strong value to members. But we do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we’re confident we’ll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing against the aforementioned strategy.
7 https://about.netflix.com/en/news/netflix-hosts-first-uk-upfront
That confidence comes from seeing strong results when we execute well on our core strategy – our business in India in Q3 is an example. We delivered a great slate led by Lock Upp, our first daily reality series, which drove the most viewing of any title on Netflix in India ever8, the new scripted series Musafir Cafe* (9M) and the hit series Operation Safed Sagar* (11M). As a result, view hours in India grew 24% year over year, while view hours per member grew low-to-mid single digits in the quarter. Combined with our first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart, we achieved our largest quarter ever of paid net additions in India and grew Q3 revenue in India ~18% year over year on a F/X neutral basis.
To close out the year, our Q4 slate builds on the strategy outlined above:
•We’ll have new series including, from the US, the critically acclaimed East of Eden and The Diplomat S4, The Body, The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey, The Hunting Wives S2, and the sixth and final season of Emily in Paris, as well as Below from Canada, Pride and Prejudice from the UK, Lupin: Part 4 from France, and The Empress S3 from Germany.
•Our film releases feature The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, starring Brad Pitt, directed by David Fincher, and written by Quentin Tarantino; Animals, starring Ben Affleck and Kerry Washington; Bad Day, starring Cameron Diaz; Steps, our new animated film featuring Ali Wong, Stephanie Hsu, and Amanda Seyfried; animated film Ray Gunn, starring Scarlett Johansson and Sam Rockwell and directed by Brad Bird; and Spain’s La Bola Negra and South Korea’s Possible Love, both of which have secured official selections as their countries’ submissions for Best International Feature Film category at the Academy Awards.
•And we have our biggest quarterly live slate to date with the NFL’s inaugural Thanksgiving Eve game (with a halftime performance by U2) and a Christmas Day doubleheader, plus the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua boxing match.
Net cash generated from operating activities was $3.2B vs. $2.8B in the prior year period. Free cash flow (FCF)9 in Q3’26 totaled $2.9B vs. $2.7B in Q3’25. We have adjusted our expected 2026 FCF forecast to approximately $12.0B (vs. our prior projection of $12.5B) due primarily to the expected closing of a real estate transaction in Q4. We continue to expect an annual cash content spend to amortization ratio of ~1.1x.
Our capital allocation approach is unchanged. We prioritize reinvestment in the business, both organically and through selective M&A, while maintaining a healthy balance sheet and ample liquidity, then returning excess cash to shareholders via repurchases. In Q3, we bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8B, our largest quarter ever of stock repurchases, and we currently have $22.3B of capacity left in our remaining authorizations. We ended Q3 with gross debt of $15.3B and cash and cash equivalents of $8.2B. Gross debt was ~$1B higher than the end of Q2, reflecting a $1B bond deal we completed during the quarter in order to fund our upcoming $1B debt maturity in Q4.

bull_case: Netflix reported a 44% year-on-year increase in third-quarter profit and an 11.8% rise in revenue, marking the lowest growth rate in three years. Netflix's Q3 revenue was $12.87 billion, beating estimates of $12.86 billion, with earnings at $0.87 per share vs $0.82 estimated. Netflix's operating margin improved to 34.6% in Q3 from 28.2% a year earlier. Netflix's free cash flow rose to $2.9B from $2.66B in Q3. Netflix's subscription churn rate was ~2% in September, the industry-low.
bear_case: Netflix lowered its 2026 advertising revenue forecast from $3 billion to approximately $2.7 billion. Netflix's advertising business is projected to deliver $300 million less than expected. Netflix reported Q4 revenue of $13.44 billion, up 11.5% year-on-year. Netflix has posted monthly subscriber losses in the US throughout 2026, with no net additions reported for any month up to September. Netflix's Q4 earnings guidance was $0.67 per share, below Wall Street's $0.73 estimate. Netflix cut about 1,000 workers in a recent round of layoffs, its biggest since 2022. Netflix's content executive shake-up included the departure of Bela Bajaria and Dan Lin, with Peter Rice named as new content chief. Netflix's US TV share (7.8%) is below YouTube's (~14%) according to Nielsen. Netflix's stock has fallen 27% year-to-date as of the report date. Netflix's 2026 full-year revenue forecast is 0.2% below prior midpoint.

reasons.day: The 44% profit jump and margin expansion provide a strong foundation, but the significant downgrade in ad revenue guidance and the first full year of US subscriber losses signal a structural shift in growth drivers. The market is pricing in these risks, making a strong bullish move unjustified.
reasons.medium: The earnings beat and margin expansion provide a positive catalyst for the medium term. The company's ability to generate strong free cash flow and maintain low churn rates suggests a resilient business model that can support a moderate bullish view.
reasons.long: The earnings beat and margin expansion provide a positive catalyst for the medium term. The company's ability to generate strong free cash flow and maintain low churn rates suggests a resilient business model that can support a moderate bullish view.
reasons.short: The loss of US subscribers is a critical weakness that directly impacts the core revenue base. While the profit jump is positive, the lack of subscriber growth in the US suggests a fundamental issue with the primary growth engine.
